title: Interpol: World Police
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss Interpol, the International Criminal Police Organization: its neutrality and mandate (terrorism, child sexual abuse, organized crime, fugitives, cybercrime, trafficking, drugs, environmental crime), how it works through National Central Bureaus rather than making arrests, its databases and 24/7 I-24/7 communications network, incident response teams for disasters like the 2004 tsunami, its structure (General Assembly, Executive Committee, Secretary General, General Secretariat in Lyon, regional offices), budget, color-coded notices (red, orange, yellow, blue, green, black, purple, and the UN Security Council special notice), its history including Nazi-era collusion, the 2009 executive order granting immunities, and notable cases such as the 2011 child pedophile ring bust and the Madrid train bombing investigation. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about beer brewing and Anheuser-Busch carbonation.

segments.title: Opening banter and 2011 pedophile ring bust
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, then discuss Interpol's March 2011 bust of a child pedophile ring centered on a forum on boylover.net, in which 232 children were rescued and 184 suspects arrested across about thirty countries.

segments.title: What Interpol is and what it does
segments.summary: Interpol is described as the International Criminal Police Organization, autonomous and not beholden to any one country, funded by member contributions. It focuses on crimes crossing borders, including terrorism, child sexual abuse, organized crime, fugitives, computer crime, money laundering, trafficking, drugs and environmental crime, and acts as a meeting point rather than making arrests itself.

segments.title: National Central Bureaus, databases and 24/7 communications
segments.summary: Interpol links national police through National Central Bureaus, using an example of an FBI agent needing Italian police help. It maintains large databases (fingerprints, DNA, wanted persons, and over twelve million lost or stolen travel documents) accessed through the I-24/7 network, which operates around the clock.

segments.title: Incident response teams and disaster work
segments.summary: Interpol can send criminal or disaster incident response teams, often coordinated through the UN, to help identify victims, find missing persons and protect children after disasters such as the 2004 Indonesian tsunami. Teams also serve as central command when local authorities request it.

segments.title: Structure, leadership and budget
segments.summary: Interpol has a General Assembly with one vote per member nation, an elected thirteen-member Executive Committee, and an elected Secretary General, currently Ronald K. Noble, an American in his third term. The General Secretariat is in Lyon, France, with regional offices including one at the UN in New York. The budget was about 61 million US dollars in 2007.

segments.title: Color-coded notices
segments.summary: Interpol issues colored notices: red for wanted persons, orange for imminent threats, yellow for missing persons, blue for individuals of interest, green for warnings about major criminals, black for unidentified bodies, and purple for criminal methods such as the pen gun. A UN Security Council special notice covers individuals sanctioned over al-Qaeda or the Taliban.

segments.title: History, Nazi-era collusion and 2009 immunity order
segments.summary: Interpol was formed in Austria and was taken over by the Nazis, who moved it to Berlin and shared headquarters with the Gestapo; wartime presidents were Nazi war criminals, and Paul Dickopf, an SS officer, was president in the 1960s and early 1970s. After the war it moved to Paris. The hosts also discuss Obama's 2009 executive order extending immunities from certain taxes, searches and seizures to Interpol, and notable successes including the Madrid train bombing and the capture of Milan Lukic and an arrest tied to Abu Musab al-Zarqawi.

segments.title: Listener mail on beer brewing
segments.summary: A listener who brews beer for Anheuser-Busch writes to correct the show's claim about forced carbonation, explaining that Budweiser is naturally carbonated during a twenty-one-day aging period. The hosts also discuss favorite beers.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give contact information for the show and sign off.
